add_eyes.name: The Indian Society of Oriental Art exhibition, Calcutta (Stella Kramrisch, Abanindranath and Gaganendranath Tagore, O. C. Ganguly)
add_eyes.role: The society's fourteenth annual exhibition and the people around it: Kramrisch, a young Austrian art historian teaching at Rabindranath Tagore's Santiniketan (1921–23), who invited the Bauhaus to send work; the Tagore brothers of the Bengal School, who showed beside it; and the critic O. C. Ganguly, who defended it in print
add_eyes.side: Indian; the Bengal School and its Calcutta public
add_eyes.vantage_label: abroad: the school's work seen in Calcutta
add_eyes.form: exhibition catalogue (December 1922), press reviews and loan lists; a collective eye like the councils
add_eyes.authenticity: The society's catalogue (December 1922) survives, and a Feininger loan list for Calcutta is in the Landesarchiv Thüringen. The best-known modern account, 'Bauhaus Calcutta' (bauhaus imaginista; first in Curating Subjects, 2007), is described by its own publisher as semi-fictional, built from the reviews and the catalogue, so its scene-setting is not used as fact here. Accounts differ on who chose the works (Kramrisch's invitation; some say Itten was asked; one says Abanindranath curated). No individual diary is known; digest only.
add_eyes.bio: In December 1922, a few months after Kandinsky reached Weimar, about 250 Bauhaus prints, drawings and watercolours hung in Calcutta opposite paintings of the Bengal School. It was the first Bauhaus showing outside Germany and the largest outside Europe in the school's lifetime. The show gives the chapter a view from outside Europe: Indian painters and critics judging Klee and Kandinsky at the moment when Indian painting was itself being renewed.

sources.title: Google Arts & Culture: How Bauhaus Found Its Way to India

add_eyes.name: Mizutani Takehiko
add_eyes.role: Japanese architecture graduate of the Tokyo School of Fine Arts on a government bursary, the first Japanese student at the Bauhaus (1927–29)
add_eyes.where: Reimann School, Berlin (1926), then Bauhaus Dessau (1927–29)
add_eyes.vantage_label: student from Japan inside the school
add_eyes.form: study records and dated works; later teaching
add_eyes.authenticity: His enrolment, courses and dates are given by Bauhaus Kooperation; preliminary-course exercises survive. No diary has been located for this chapter; his life dates are not confirmed here.
add_eyes.bio: Mizutani took the preliminary course under Josef Albers and László Moholy-Nagy and then worked in the furniture workshop and the building department. Back in Tokyo he co-founded a research institute for design in 1931 and taught at Kawakita Renshichirō's Shinkenchiku Kōgei Gakuin, which carried Bauhaus teaching into Japan.

sources.title: Bauhaus Kooperation: From Dessau to Tokyo
AIGA Eye on Design: From Weimar to Tokyo

add_eyes.name: Yamawaki Iwao (born Fujita Iwao)
add_eyes.role: Japanese architect, about 32 on arrival; student of Mies van der Rohe, Ludwig Hilberseimer and the photographer Walter Peterhans, 1930–32
add_eyes.where: Bauhaus Dessau, winter semester 1930 to summer semester 1932
add_eyes.form: dated letters and reports to Japan; photomontage; memoirs (written later)
add_eyes.authenticity: His letters to Japan (21 December 1930, 24 March 1931) and his 'Report C' on the closure (4 September 1932) are cited with dates in the bauhaus imaginista essay on his collage. His books on the Bauhaus (1942, 1954, 1973) are later memoirs and are flagged. Digest only.
add_eyes.bio: Yamawaki took his wife's family name on their arranged marriage in 1928, which paid for study abroad. At Dessau he studied architecture and photography and wrote home about the school. When the Dessau council closed it, he built a photomontage from a Berlin newspaper's report, The Attack on the Bauhaus, and sent it to a Tokyo architecture magazine: the closure as seen and published from Japan.

sources.title: bauhaus imaginista: The Attack on the Bauhaus
Bauhaus Kooperation: From Dessau to Tokyo

add_eyes.name: Yamawaki Michiko
add_eyes.role: Weaving student, aged 20 on arrival; daughter of a Tokyo tea master
add_eyes.authenticity: Her account, Bauhausu to chanoyu (The Bauhaus and the Tea Ceremony, Shinchōsha, 1995), was written more than sixty years later and is flagged wherever used. Bauhaus Kooperation gives her return to Japan as 1932 in one article and 1933 in her biography. Digest only.
add_eyes.bio: After the preliminary course Yamawaki Michiko trained in the weaving workshop under Gunta Stölzl and Otti Berger, and she recalled Albers and Kandinsky explaining lessons to the couple in English after class. She took two looms home to Tokyo, headed the weaving class at the Shinkenchiku Kōgei Gakuin in 1934 and taught modern design at Shōwa Women's University from 1960. Her memoir sets the Bauhaus beside the tea ceremony she grew up with.

sources.title: bauhaus imaginista: The Bauhaus and the Tea Ceremony

add_entries.headline: Klee and Kandinsky hang opposite the Bengal School
add_entries.digest: The Indian Society of Oriental Art opened its fourteenth annual exhibition with about 250 works lent from Weimar: watercolours, drawings and woodcuts by Klee, Kandinsky, Feininger and Itten, with student work. They hung on one side of the hall, facing paintings by Abanindranath and Gaganendranath Tagore, Nandalal Bose and others. Stella Kramrisch, teaching at Santiniketan, had invited the school to send them. Rabindranath Tagore is said to have attended, and the society printed a catalogue whose essay made a lyrical case for the Germans.
add_entries.source_note: Month, venue, scale and artists: bauhaus imaginista 'Bauhaus Calcutta' and Google Arts & Culture story. The exact opening day is not given in either source, and the opening-ceremony scene comes from an essay its publisher calls semi-fictional, so it is not used.

add_entries.headline: Ganguly defends the Bauhaus; almost nothing sells
add_entries.digest: O. C. Ganguly, the critic, wrote in defence of the Bauhaus work for Bengali readers. Other reviewers called it ugly, incomprehensible or subversive, and some asked why European art was being shown just as Indian painting was being renewed. The works were offered for sale at about ten pounds each, and one account says only one was sold.
add_entries.source_note: Reception: bauhaus imaginista 'Bauhaus Calcutta' (reviews summarised, not dated). Price and the single sale: Nonie Niesewand, Seminar 2019, citing Partha Mitter, The Triumph of Modernism; not checked against the catalogue.

add_entries.headline: The first Japanese student enrols at Dessau
add_entries.digest: After a year at Berlin's Reimann School, Mizutani Takehiko transferred to the Bauhaus. He took the preliminary course taught by Josef Albers and László Moholy-Nagy, folding and cutting paper and studying materials, and then joined the furniture workshop and the new building department under Hannes Meyer.
add_entries.source_note: Bauhaus Kooperation, 'From Dessau to Tokyo' (enrolled 1927; preliminary course with Albers and Moholy-Nagy; furniture workshop and building department).

add_entries.headline: Mizutani carries the preliminary course home
add_entries.digest: Mizutani left the Bauhaus in 1929 and was back in Japan in 1930. In 1931 he co-founded a research institute for everyday design with Kawakita Renshichirō, and he then taught at Kawakita's new school in Tokyo, where Bauhaus-style exercises became part of Japanese art education.
add_entries.source_note: Bauhaus Kooperation, 'From Dessau to Tokyo' (left 1929; returned 1930; institute 1931; taught at the Shinkenchiku Kōgei Gakuin).

add_entries.headline: A tea master's daughter enters the preliminary course
add_entries.digest: Michiko and Iwao Yamawaki began the winter semester at Dessau, under Mies van der Rohe's directorship. They spoke little German, and she later recalled Albers and Kandinsky going over the lessons with them in English after class. The account comes from her memoir of 1995 and is a late recollection.
add_entries.source_note: Bauhaus Kooperation biography (winter semester 1930; English explanations from Albers and Kandinsky); Bauhausu to chanoyu (1995), a memoir written later. Start of semester assumed to be October.

add_entries.headline: A letter home about buying a large camera
add_entries.digest: Two months into the school, Yamawaki wrote to Japan about buying a large-format camera. Alongside architecture he was taking Walter Peterhans's photography course, and the camera became one of his main tools at the school.
add_entries.source_note: bauhaus imaginista, 'The Attack on the Bauhaus' (letter dated 21 December 1930 cited); his studies with Peterhans from Bauhaus Kooperation.

add_entries.headline: Reporting on the advertising and photography classes
add_entries.digest: Yamawaki sent Japan an account of the Bauhaus classes in advertising and photography, describing the teaching for readers who knew the school only from magazines. He was studying architecture with Mies and Hilberseimer as well.
add_entries.source_note: bauhaus imaginista, 'The Attack on the Bauhaus' (letter dated 24 March 1931 cited); courses from Bauhaus Kooperation.

add_entries.headline: At the looms under Stölzl and Otti Berger
add_entries.digest: Michiko Yamawaki moved from the preliminary course into the weaving workshop, taught by Gunta Stölzl until Stölzl left in 1931 and then by Otti Berger. She learned to weave on the workshop's looms, two of which the couple later shipped to Tokyo for her studio.
add_entries.source_note: Bauhaus Kooperation biography (teachers Stölzl and Berger) and 'From Dessau to Tokyo' (two looms brought home). The year of her move into the workshop is inferred, not stated.

add_entries.headline: 'Report C': the closure written up for Tokyo
add_entries.digest: Less than two weeks after the Dessau council voted to close the school, Yamawaki sent Japan a report on the closure. Around the same time he made his photomontage from Berlin newspaper coverage of 7 and 23 August: built around a bird's-eye photograph of the Bauhaus balconies, under a title taken from a Berlin headline.
add_entries.source_note: bauhaus imaginista, 'The Attack on the Bauhaus' (Report C dated 4 September 1932; source articles of 7 and 23 August 1932; collage of 1932).

add_entries.headline: The Attack on the Bauhaus published in Tokyo
add_entries.digest: Yamawaki's collage Der Schlag gegen das Bauhaus appeared in the Tokyo architecture magazine Kokusai Kenchiku. Japanese readers thus saw the closure of Dessau as a montage made by a student who had been there. The Yamawakis went home with furniture, books and looms instead of following Mies to Berlin.
add_entries.source_note: bauhaus imaginista, 'The Attack on the Bauhaus' (Kokusai Kenchiku vol. 8 no. 12, December 1932; page numbers given differently in two places). Return: Bauhaus Kooperation (1932 in one article, 1933 in the biography).

add_convergences.label: December 1922: the Bauhaus in Calcutta
add_convergences.note: None of the four masters went to India, but their prints and watercolours hung in Park Street opposite the Bengal School, half a year after Kandinsky arrived in Weimar. The Calcutta critics divided, as the Weimar Landtag soon would: Ganguly defended the work, while others called it ugly or beside the point for an India renewing its own art.

add_convergences.label: August–December 1932: the closure seen from Dessau and Tokyo
add_convergences.note: The council's 20-to-5 vote, which Mies answered by moving the school to Berlin, reached Japan through Yamawaki's report of 4 September and his montage published in December. For the two Japanese students the vote ended their studies: they went home rather than follow Mies to the telephone factory in Steglitz.

add_ties.note: Married in 1928; they studied at Dessau together from the winter semester of 1930 and took the school's methods and two looms back to Tokyo.
Yamawaki studied architecture in Mies van der Rohe's class at Dessau, 1930–32.
Stölzl taught her weaving in the Dessau workshop before leaving in 1931; Otti Berger continued the teaching.
Itten's work was in the Calcutta show; one account says Kramrisch asked him to send the 250 works but the sources disagree on who chose them.

add_threads_out.note: The Calcutta show of December 1922 came out of the Tagore circle: Stella Kramrisch was teaching at Rabindranath Tagore's Santiniketan, and his nephews Abanindranath and Gaganendranath hung their paintings opposite the Bauhaus work. The link is usually traced to Tagore's 1921 visit to Germany.

After his dismissal as Bauhaus director and his years in Moscow, Hannes Meyer emigrated to Mexico in 1939, taught there and worked with the Taller de Gráfica Popular, the print workshop that grew out of the muralists' tradition of public political art.

fix.vantage_key: 0 = director or principal actor in a decision; 1 = master, student or household member inside the school; 2 = the councils and press that funded and judged it; 4 = abroad (the Calcutta exhibition of 1922).

updates.why: The new Calcutta eye uses vantage 4, so the old wording 'none used here' would become wrong.
